grossMargin.title: Gross Margin
grossMargin.content:
Gross profit (revenue less cost of goods sold) as a percentage of revenue.

For Synlait: gross margin ran 12-19% through FY2015-FY2020 during the a2 Milk exclusivity era when Advanced Nutrition base-powder volumes were high and well-utilised. It has never recovered to those levels post-exclusivity and turned NEGATIVE in H1 FY2026 (-0.2%) -- the company lost money on cost of goods sold alone, before any overheads, interest or tax.

What to watch:

  • Whether the South-Island-only, post-Abbott-sale cost base (lower fixed-cost drag without the loss-making North Island plant) lifts margin back into positive territory in H2 FY2026 and FY2027
  • Milk price pass-through -- a2 Milk base-powder contracts are largely fixed-margin, so a high milk price (FY2025's record $10.16/kgMS) compresses margin on the Ingredients (commodity) side
  • Whether the FY25-HY26 one-off costs (NZ$33m tactical raw-milk losses, NZ$43.5m manufacturing plan adjustment) wash out of the cost base as management guides

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation.

For Synlait: EBITDA went negative in FY2021 (-$28.5m -> actually -17.7m EBIT, EBITDA still positive at $32.6m) and again in FY2024 (-$126.8m), the depth of the 2023-24 solvency crisis that forced the Sept-2024 Bright Dairy/a2 Milk recapitalisation. FY2025 recovered to a modest $44.2m.

What to watch:

  • FY bars vs H1 bars are NOT comparable -- an H1 bar covers six months, an FY bar covers twelve
  • The base-case DCF assumes EBITDA margin ramps from ~3.5% to 6.5% by FY2032 -- well below the 12-16% margins of the a2-exclusivity era, because a2 Milk now takes only minimum committed volumes
  • Whether the going-concern material-uncertainty paragraph (live on the latest reviewed accounts) is lifted, which management has said requires "sustained improvement"

netIncome.title: Net Income
netIncome.content:
Bottom-line profit or loss after interest, tax and all items.

For Synlait: guided at a third consecutive underlying loss for FY2026 (NZ$19-24m), following a $182.1m FY2024 loss (the solvency-crisis low point) and a $39.8m FY2025 loss. H1 FY2026 alone lost $80.6m reported / $27.3m underlying.

What to watch:

  • The gap between reported and underlying loss (one-off restructuring, impairment and manufacturing-plan-adjustment costs)
  • Whether H2 FY2026 narrows the loss as guided, aided by the 1-Apr-2026 Abbott sale removing the loss-making North Island business for a full quarter
  • CEO Richard Wyeth resigned May-2026 after 11 months; the seat is empty going into the FY2026 result -- leadership stability is itself a risk factor priced into the DCF's 40% bear weight

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Total sales across Advanced Nutrition, Ingredients, Dairyworks (Consumer) and Foodservice.

For Synlait: revenue growth here is largely a milk-price and product-mix story, not volume growth -- FY2025's record $10.16/kgMS milk price inflated ingredients revenue even as underlying volumes were weak. Includes the North Island (Pokeno) business through FY2025/H1 FY2026, sold to Abbott 1-Apr-2026, so FY2027 revenue will step down on a like-for-like basis.

What to watch:

  • Segment mix shift: Dairyworks/Consumer (+51% HY26) and Foodservice (+48% HY26, turned profitable) are growing; Ingredients volume is down 25%
  • China revenue share rose from 7% (HY25) to 18% (HY26) as North Island Yashili-style volumes wound down and Dunsandel-made product grew
  • Post-Abbott-sale, revenue is 100% South-Island (Dunsandel) sourced -- a smaller, more concentrated base

debtCash.title: Total Debt vs Cash
debtCash.content:
Gross borrowings and cash on hand, the two inputs to net debt.

For Synlait: total debt at 31-Jan-2026 was $504.4m (RCF $273m + term loans $72m + NZD/CNH $29.4m + the Bright Dairy $130m shareholder loan), all classified current because the facilities matured 30-Jun-2026 and the shareholder loan matures 12-Jul-2026 with refinancing only "preliminarily indicated," not confirmed, in the last filing.

What to watch:

  • Whether the syndicate refinances the (post-Abbott-sale, roughly halved) bank facilities and Bright Dairy rolls its shareholder loan -- the base case assumes both happen with no further equity raise
  • Cash is highly seasonal (dairy season working-capital cycle), so a single balance-sheet date can overstate or understate the underlying position

equity.title: Shareholders' Equity
equity.content:
Total assets less total liabilities -- the book value cushion available to equity holders.

For Synlait: equity fell from $830m (H1 2021) to $605m (FY2024) through the solvency crisis, then was rebuilt to ~$789m by FY2025 almost entirely by two dilutive capital raises (NZ$200m Nov-2020, ~NZ$212m net Oct-2024) against ~NZ$216m of cumulative FY2021-FY2025 net losses -- the 5-year equity CAGR of +5.4% is raise-funded, not organic profit growth.

What to watch:

  • Whether FY2027+ profits can sustain or grow equity without a third raise
  • The DCF's bear case is a genuine equity-impairment path where enterprise value fails to cover net debt (implied intrinsic value -$0.111/share) -- not a low multiple, an under-water balance sheet

shares.title: Shares Outstanding
shares.content:
Total ordinary shares on issue.

For Synlait: the Sept/Oct-2024 recapitalisation nearly tripled the count from 218.6m to 603.2m, issued to Bright Dairy (now 65.25% owner) and a2 Milk (19.83%) at NZ$0.60 and NZ$0.43 respectively -- roughly 50% above the then market price for Bright's tranche. Yahoo Finance historical prices are NOT adjusted for this placement, which is why the DCF's historical multiples are shown on a market-cap basis rather than per-share.

What to watch:

  • Any further dilutive raise if the FY2026 refinancing requires one
  • The 85% combined Bright Dairy/a2 Milk stake means minority holders' realised value depends on those two shareholders' decisions, which the DCF explicitly does not assume will favour minorities

fcf.title: Operating Cash Flow vs Free Cash Flow
fcf.content:
OCF is cash generated by operations; FCF deducts capital expenditure.

For Synlait: both series are dominated by capex supercycles (FY2019's -$320m Pokeno build) and working-capital swings (FY2022 and FY2025 both had +$135-142m releases; H1 FY2026 alone was a -$199.8m build). The 10-year median owner FCF (after stripping SBC, interest income and IFRS-16 lease principal) is NEGATIVE -$27.1m -- reported FCF materially overstates underlying cash generation in the good years.

What to watch:

  • The DCF does NOT extrapolate from this series -- it builds forward FCF bottom-up from revenue x margin path x capex x working capital, precisely because this history is too volatile to trend
  • H2 FY2026 cash flow, given the seasonal working-capital unwind embedded in the DCF's net-debt estimate

capex.title: Capital Expenditure
capex.content:
Cash spent on property, plant, equipment and intangibles.

For Synlait: FY2019's -$320m capex peak funded the Pokeno (North Island) plant, sold to Abbott 1-Apr-2026 for ~NZ$307m gross -- so that investment cycle is now largely reversed. Post-sale, the DCF assumes maintenance-only capex (~1.8% of revenue) against a ~$600m PP&E base, with no further growth projects.

What to watch:

  • Whether capex stays at maintenance levels or any new growth capex (Dairyworks expansion, Foodservice capacity) is announced

eps.title: Earnings Per Share (cents)
eps.content:
Net income divided by weighted average shares outstanding, in NZ cents.

For Synlait: EPS is reported in CENTS, not dollars. The Sept-2024 share count near-tripling (218.6m to 603.2m) mechanically depresses post-recap EPS relative to pre-recap EPS for any given profit level -- a loss of the same dollar magnitude now produces roughly one-third the per-share impact it would have pre-recap, and vice versa for profits. EPS CAGRs are undefined across this history because of the FY2021, FY2023-FY2025 losses.

What to watch:

  • Treat pre-Sept-2024 and post-Sept-2024 EPS as two different regimes, never one continuous trend line
  • FY-only chart (interim EPS half-years are not shown here to avoid a misleading annualisation)
